The city is called something like Ambré, or possibly Amberly — you can never check, because every sign in it is written in a script that resolves into legibility only when you look away. You know the name the way you know a word in a language you spoke fluently last night.

Roll onto your right and the harbor is behind you, and the city climbs instead, into terraces of apartment buildings whose windows are all lit the same warm yellow, all of them, and none of them occupied by anyone you can name.

The architecture is made of the last thing you thought about before sleep. If you fell asleep worrying about money, the buildings are banks — not real banks, but the idea of banks: columns, marble, a queue that moves without anyone stepping forward. If you fell asleep mid-sentence, the buildings are made of that sentence, and you can walk through its rooms, and each room is a clause, and the furniture is the pause before the verb.

There's a market. It sells things you almost remember wanting. A woman hands you a paper cone of something hot — chestnuts, maybe, or the smell of chestnuts, which is different. You eat it and it tastes like the first cold day of a year you can't place. You try to thank her and find you've been talking to her for an hour, or for no time at all.

The light is the light of a room you're not in. It comes from the next room over, through a door left ajar, and it's always the color of a television left on, or a hallway at 4 a.m., or the underside of a lampshade. There are no shadows exactly; there are just places where the light is more certain of itself.

Sound behaves strangely. A dog barks three streets away and it's the bark of a dog you had as a child, and you know it's that dog, and you also know it's just a dog. A radio plays in a kitchen — a song you can hum but not name, with a chorus that arrives just as you're about to predict it. Someone is walking up stairs. They have been walking up the stairs the whole time you've been here. They will arrive when you stop listening.

The people are the people you almost know. Your mother is there, but she's the age she was in a photograph you saw once, and she's busy, and she'll talk to you in a minute. A friend you haven't thought about in years stands at a crossing, waiting for a light that doesn't change. You call out, and your voice comes out as the feeling of having called out.

You can't read. Not because the words are foreign, but because reading requires a stillness this city doesn't have. You can hold a newspaper and understand it completely, and the moment you try to say what it said, it becomes a menu, then a receipt, then a map of the city, which is also a map of your hand.

The city has a river. Everyone says so. You've never seen it, but you've crossed it many times — you know this from the slight rise and fall of the bridge, the change in the sound of your footsteps, the way the air goes cold and mineral for exactly eleven steps.

It ends the way it begins: not with a fade but with a correction. You'll be standing in the Almost Market, holding something, and you'll notice the light has become the light of your own room, and the market is your ceiling, and the thing in your hand is the corner of your pillow.
